title: Undertow and Radiators
premise: Petra Whitlock, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through the hum of its radiators, has spent thirty years keeping an inventory of everything unsaid—about the summer her friend Ingrid drowned, about the language their grandmother spoke in secret, about why Petra left the coastal village of Skarvik and never went back. When Edda Lindqvist, the last fluent speaker of that dying language, asks Petra to become her final student before Edda's memory fails, Petra must return to Skarvik, where the radiator-song of her childhood home still accuses her. Learning the language forces Petra to hear, at last, what was actually said the night Ingrid died—and to discover that Ingrid's death was an accident Petra's silence helped turn into a story that destroyed an innocent man. In the end, Petra speaks the true account aloud in the village church, in the old language, accepting exile from the community's forgiveness but winning back her own name.
about_author: Astrid Eriksen is the pen name of a former interpreter who grew up in a bilingual household on the Baltic coast and spent a decade documenting endangered dialects before turning to fiction. She lives above a piano workshop, where she claims the radiators tell her when it will snow.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In her city apartment, Petra tunes a client's piano while cataloguing, in her notebook, the silences she maintains: about her sister, her village, her mother tongue. A letter arrives from a stranger named Edda Lindqvist. The beat is controlled loneliness—the reader senses a dammed river.

chapters.title: A Language with One Throat Left
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra visits Edda in a care home; the old woman speaks a language Petra hasn't heard in thirty years and asks for one final student before her dementia erases her. Petra refuses and leaves. Emotional beat: terror disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Back home, Petra tunes a Victorian house and hears, in its pipes, the echo of her grandmother's kitchen in Skarvik—the same rhythm, the same argument in the walls. She begins translating her notebook of silences into the old language. Beat: the past becoming audible.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Edda's second letter contains a photograph of Petra and Ingrid at fourteen, and one sentence in the old tongue Petra cannot make herself translate. She books a train to Skarvik. Beat: the first crack in thirty years of stillness.

chapters.title: Skarvik in the Off-Season
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra arrives in the shuttered coastal village; the house where she grew up is a rental now, but the radiators still sing the same three-note warning. She is recognized by the fishmonger, who calls her by Ingrid's name by mistake. Beat: displacement and dread.

chapters.title: Lessons in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, with Edda's voice threaded in. First lessons: Edda teaches through objects and refuses to translate the word for the thing Ingrid died near. Petra realizes the language has no future tense. Beat: tenderness laced with evasion.

chapters.title: The Man Who Stayed Guilty
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In the village shop, Petra encounters Halvard Nilsen, the man convicted—by rumor, never by law—of causing Ingrid's drowning. He is old now, diminished, and he thanks her for coming back. Beat: guilt with a human face.

chapters.title: Ingrid, Swimming
chapters.summary: Petra's POV in extended flashback. Fourteen-year-old Petra and Ingrid on the last golden day, speaking the secret language their grandmother taught them, Ingrid daring Petra to swim past the breakwater. Petra said no. Ingrid went alone. Beat: the reader finally sees the wound.

chapters.title: What Petra Told the Constable
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, flashback. The interrogation after the drowning: Petra, terrified, describes Halvard's boat near the breakwater—a detail she invented to end the questioning. Her mother, listening through the door, says nothing. Beat: the origin of the inventory.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Punishment
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, flashback. After Ingrid's death, Petra's grandmother was forbidden to speak the old language—blamed for filling the girls' heads with secrets. Petra watched the language be buried and chose exile over witness. Beat: complicity inherited.

chapters.title: Edda's Missing Year
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra asks Edda about the summer of the drowning; Edda's memory flickers and she reveals she was Ingrid's tutor that year—the language lesson Ingrid was walking home from when she went to the water. Beat: the two silences begin to interlock.

chapters.title: The Radiator Song of the Church
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Hired to tune the church piano, Petra hears in the building's pipes a rhythm she recognizes from Edda's lessons: a lament for the drowned. The village's grief and its lie share one melody. Beat: the truth becoming inescapable.

chapters.title: Halvard's Version
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Halvard. Halvard, tending his nets, recalls the day Ingrid drowned—how his boat drifted engineless, how he screamed himself hoarse, how the village decided anyway. He has kept Ingrid's lost scarf for thirty years. Beat: sympathy for the accused.

chapters.title: The Word Edda Refused
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Edda, in a lucid window, finally teaches the forbidden word: it means both 'undertow' and 'the truth that pulls you back.' Petra understands the language itself has been waiting for her confession. Beat: epiphany.

chapters.title: Petra's Mother Returns
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Solveig, Petra's mother. Solveig arrives for Edda's sake, and mother and daughter circle each other with teacups and knives. Solveig admits she heard Petra's lie in 1989 and chose the village's peace over her daughter's soul. Beat: the second confession begins.

chapters.title: Edda Forgets the Alphabet
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Edda's dementia accelerates; she begins losing the language mid-sentence, and Petra must record everything, racing the tide of forgetting. Edda mistakes Petra for Ingrid and begs her not to swim. Beat: urgency sharpening into desperation.

chapters.title: The Scarf on the Doorstep
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Halvard leaves Ingrid's scarf at Petra's door with a note: 'Tell them what you told me, or I will die with it.' Petra realizes he has known her lie for decades and stayed silent to protect a child. Beat: the last shield removed.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra walks the breakwater at night, hears the radiator-song of the empty village like a held breath, and drafts—then burns—three versions of a confession. She decides the truth must be spoken aloud, in the old language, where the lie was born. Beat: resolve.

chapters.title: Sunday, in the Old Tongue
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. At the church service, Petra stands during the hymn and tells the whole truth in the dying language—Edda beside her, translating into Norwegian for the stunned congregation. She names her lie, names Halvard's innocence, names her own cowardice. Beat: climax, raw and public.

chapters.title: The Village Answers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Halvard, then the fishmonger. The village fractures—anger at Petra, shame at itself. Some turn away; the fishmonger, who lost a cousin to the same rumor mill, is the first to shake Halvard's hand. Beat: aftermath, neither absolution nor ruin.

chapters.title: Edda's Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Edda, nearly wordless now, teaches Petra one final construction: the old language's way of saying 'I was there, and it was not your fault, and it was.' Petra records it. Edda dies that night with Petra speaking to her in their grandmother's tongue. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance.

chapters.title: Undertow and Radiators
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra stays in Skarvik, tuning pianos along the coast, her notebook now an inventory of things said. The house's radiators sing a new note—three notes, resolved. She begins teaching the language to two village children. Beat: quiet redemption; the language, like Petra, survives by being spoken.
